# California Didn't Lose Larry Page When He Left. It Lost Him the Moment the Proposal Was Written.

That distinction matters more than most people realize.

Paul Graham recently noted that Larry Page has genuinely relocated out of California — not a paper move, not a part-time arrangement. A full, permanent departure. And here's the part that should stop every founder and policymaker cold: no wealth tax has even passed yet.

The threat alone was enough.

---

**Credible policy risk is functionally identical to enacted policy.**

High-net-worth individuals and the advisors who serve them don't wait for the bill to become law. They model scenarios. They assess probability-weighted outcomes. And when the calculus tips past a certain threshold, they move — quietly, efficiently, and permanently. By the time the legislation clears a committee, the capital is already gone. California isn't losing tax revenue in the future. It lost it the moment the proposal gained traction.

This is the fundamental miscalculation embedded in every aggressive wealth tax proposal: the assumption that the asset stays put while you debate the rate.

---

**The behavioral response is the data point, not the legislation.**

Policymakers tend to model tax revenue as if human beings are passive inputs in a spreadsheet. They're not. Founders, operators, and capital allocators are the most mobile people on earth. They've already built the optionality — multiple residencies, distributed teams, remote infrastructure — that makes relocation frictionless. California built its entire fiscal identity around a tax base that was always one policy decision away from relocating.

Larry Page's move isn't an outlier. It's a leading indicator.

---

**For founders still in California, this is a jurisdiction risk conversation, not a lifestyle one.**

I've had this conversation with multiple operators in the last 12 months. The question used to be: "Would you ever leave?" Now it's: "What's your threshold?" That shift in framing is significant. Founders are actively building exit optionality into their long-term planning — not because they want to leave, but because the policy environment has made it strategically irresponsible not to.

If you're building a company with a 10+ year horizon and your domicile strategy doesn't account for jurisdiction risk, you're not thinking like a founder. You're thinking like a resident.

---

**Texas, Florida, and Nevada didn't steal California's talent. California is handing it over.**

No aggressive recruiting campaign, no incentive package, no marketing effort from competing states produced what a single wealth tax proposal in Sacramento achieved. The exit velocity is self-generated. And unlike a competitor you can out-execute, you cannot out-compete your own government's policy decisions.

The compounding effect here is what keeps me up at night: it's not just the capital that leaves. It's the networks, the pattern-matching, the deal flow, the next company that gets funded because the founder stayed in the room. That's not quantifiable on a spreadsheet, but it's the most valuable thing any innovation ecosystem has.

---

California has the talent, the infrastructure, the culture, and the universities to be the dominant technology jurisdiction for the next 50 years. But none of that is immune to sustained policy pressure.

Larry Page leaving before a law passes is the cleanest signal you'll see that the window for course correction is shorter than Sacramento thinks.

**Founders: have you had the jurisdiction risk conversation with your co-founders and board yet? If not — why not?**
source_story_title: Larry Page Permanently Leaves California Amid Wealth Tax Threat
source_story_summary: Paul Graham reports that Larry Page has genuinely relocated out of California — not merely established nominal residency in Florida — before any wealth tax legislation has even passed. Graham frames this as a concrete, early cost to California: the physical departure of a billionaire and the complete loss of associated tax revenue, serving as a cautionary data point about the real behavioral effects of proposed wealth taxes.

# The 1,000-Line-Per-Hour Engineer Isn't Coming. They're Already Here.

Six months ago, Paul Graham shared a data point about AI-assisted coding productivity and got an even split: half the room believed it, half didn't. He just ran the same test again. The implication is obvious — the skeptics are running out of cover.

An experienced programmer hitting roughly 1,000 lines of AI-assisted code per hour is no longer a party trick. It's becoming a baseline expectation. And if your team hasn't internalized what that means for how you build, hire, and compete, you're already behind.

Here's what I'm watching closely:

**The productivity gap is now a structural gap.**

This isn't about individual engineers being more productive in isolation. It's about what a small, focused team can now ship in a quarter versus what used to require a full engineering department. The ceiling on what a lean founding team can execute has moved dramatically. The floor for what investors and customers expect has moved with it. Teams not integrating AI coding tools aren't just slower — they're operating with a fundamentally different cost structure than their competition.

**Fewer engineers doesn't mean weaker teams. It means higher signal density.**

If one experienced engineer can now output what three were shipping before, the hiring calculus changes completely. Not because you eliminate headcount, but because every seat on the team carries more weight. The bar for what "good" looks like goes up. You stop optimizing for coverage and start optimizing for sharpness. The best founding teams are already making this shift — building smaller, moving faster, and compressing timelines that would have been impossible 18 months ago.

**Acceptance is the leading indicator, not adoption.**

The more interesting signal in Graham's post isn't the productivity number itself — it's that the response to the same data point has shifted from contested to normalized. That's how mainstream adoption actually moves. Not with a formal announcement, but with a quiet change in what people are willing to argue against. When experienced engineers stop pushing back on these figures, the tools become table stakes. We're at that inflection point right now.

**The uncomfortable question for operators: what are you doing with the recaptured time?**

More output per engineer-hour only creates value if it's directed at the right problems. The teams winning right now aren't just shipping more code — they're using the recaptured capacity to iterate on product decisions faster, tighten feedback loops with users, and move into adjacent surfaces they couldn't have touched before. Productivity gains mean nothing if the strategy absorbing them is weak.

---

Here's where I land: the 1,000-line-per-hour figure will stop being remarkable within 12 months. It will just be what competent AI-assisted engineering looks like. The gap being created right now isn't between engineers who use AI and those who don't. It's between organizations that have restructured around this new reality and those still treating it as a feature of individual workflows.

Build for the new floor, not the old ceiling.

**If your team is integrating AI coding tools, what's the actual bottleneck you've hit — the tooling, the culture, or the strategic clarity on where to direct the output?**
source_story_title: AI Coding Productivity Hits ~1,000 Lines Per Hour for Experienced Programmers
source_story_summary: Paul Graham relays a data point from an experienced programmer achieving roughly 1,000 lines of AI-assisted code per hour, and notes that when he shared a similar statistic six months ago the response was evenly split between skepticism and validation. He is now testing whether professional acceptance of these productivity figures has shifted, implying mainstream adoption may be normalizing what was once contested.
